soil-water-001.title: Soil erosion and the 75 billion tons lost each year
soil-water-001.text: About 75 billion tons of soil are eroded from the land each year. Soil erosion is the wearing away of the upper layer of soil, a form of {{ref:soil-env-058}}. It is driven by erosive agents: water, ice, snow, wind, plants such as uprooted trees, and animals, including humans. Each agent names a type. There is erosion by water, by ice (glacial), by snow and by wind (aeolian), erosion by animals (zoogenic), and human-caused erosion such as {{ref:soil-water-038}}. Erosion can go on slowly and almost unnoticed, or fast enough to cause a serious loss of topsoil. People have sped it up. Human activities have raised the rate worldwide to about 28 times the natural rate, though other estimates in the sources run from 10 to 40 times. On site, accelerated erosion lowers farm productivity. By stripping the nutrient-rich upper layers it can collapse whole ecosystems, sometimes ending in {{ref:soil-env-072}}. Off site, it silts waterways, feeds {{ref:soil-env-020}} of lakes and rivers, and damages roads and houses with sediment. Erosion by water and wind together accounts for about 84% of the world's degraded land. One global model puts the yearly loss to water alone at almost 36 billion tons.

soil-water-003.title: Water erosion, from raindrop to gully
soil-water-003.text: By one global model's estimate, almost 36 billion tons of soil wash away every year. Water erosion is the removal of soil by rainfall and the surface runoff it produces. Runoff begins when the soil is saturated or when rain falls faster than water can infiltrate. If the flow has enough energy, it carries loosened soil particles down the slope as sediment. Rain and runoff cause four main types of erosion. In rising order of severity they are {{ref:soil-water-004}}, {{ref:soil-water-005}}, {{ref:soil-water-025}} and {{ref:soil-water-027}}. The progression is easy to follow. Concentrated runoff cuts small channels, and if it keeps deepening them they may grow into much larger ones. Water does not take soil evenly from a slope. It removes it mainly from the middle and lower parts, not from the hilltops. The bare hilltops seen in many fields have a different cause, explored in {{ref:soil-water-038}}.

soil-water-011.title: Rainfall erosivity, the striking power of rain
soil-water-011.text: Not all rain is equally destructive. Rainfall erosivity is the power of rainfall to cause erosion, set mainly by how much rain falls and how intensely. It is the main climatic control on water erosion, especially where the soil surface lacks plant cover. Larger, faster raindrops carry more kinetic energy and throw soil particles further than small, slow ones. In places such as the Midwestern United States and the Amazon, intensity matters most. Western Europe is different. There, erosion follows gentle, low-intensity stratiform rain, the steady rain of layered clouds, falling on soil that is already saturated. Total rainfall counts for more than intensity. Erosivity is the R factor of the {{ref:soil-water-041}}. The Global Rainfall Erosivity Database, GloREDa, covers 3,625 stations in 63 countries and was used to map erosivity worldwide at about 1 km resolution.

soil-water-010.title: Wind erosion and the bouncing grain
soil-water-010.text: In a drought year on the Great Plains, wind erosion losses can be up to 6100 times greater than in a wet year. Wind erosion is erosion by wind, and it works in two ways. {{ref:soil-water-030}} lifts and carries away loose particles. Abrasion wears down surfaces with windborne grains. It is a major force shaping landscapes, especially in arid and semi-arid regions. That lifting moves particles in three ways. Surface creep rolls or slides them. {{ref:soil-water-251}} sends them in short, bouncing hops. Suspension lifts fine particles and carries them far. The hopping does most of the work, 50 to 70%, followed by suspension at 30 to 40% and surface creep at 5 to 25%. Silty soils such as loess suffer most, because silt particles detach and travel easily. Wind erosion needs strong winds and is worst in drought. It is worsened by {{ref:soil-agri-095}}, which dries and breaks up the soil, and clearing trees from fields gives the wind long, open runs. Where deforestation, urbanization and farming have raised it above natural rates, it drives the decline of land, the spread of desert, harmful airborne dust and crop damage. Plants shelter the soil. Rows of trees and shrubs along field edges significantly reduce wind erosion, as {{ref:soil-agri-061}} explains.

soil-water-050.title: Erosion control, from terraces to riprap
soil-water-050.text: One of the best defenses against erosion is thousands of years old: {{ref:soil-agri-073}}, practiced around the world and still extremely effective. Erosion control is the practice of preventing or controlling wind and water erosion in farming, land development, coastal areas, river banks and construction. Good controls manage surface runoff and help prevent water pollution, soil loss, habitat loss and property damage. Many are physical barriers of vegetation or rock that absorb some of the energy of the wind or water. On farms, the methods include {{ref:soil-agri-004}}, {{ref:soil-agri-099}}, {{ref:soil-agri-123}} and {{ref:soil-agri-066}}, along with hydroseeding, streamside buffers, alternating crop strips and rows of sheltering trees. Crop leftovers on the surface soften raindrop impact, and the fibrous roots of forage crops anchor the topsoil. Mixing crops with trees works well, especially in rainy tropical climates and on severely degraded land. On construction sites, erosion controls are paired with controls on sediment such as {{ref:soil-water-099}} and {{ref:soil-water-093}}. In towns, they are part of stormwater programs. Bank erosion is natural, but where people want to hold a river in place, they line its banks with riprap or gabions.

soil-water-012.title: Why plant cover is the best shield against erosion
soil-water-012.text: Raindrops regain terminal velocity within about 8 meters, so drops falling from a tall canopy can still strike the ground at full speed. The leaves alone do not save a forest's soil. The forest floor does. Its litter and humus absorb the impact of the drops and let water percolate slowly. More than the canopy, the floor prevents surface erosion. Vegetation cover and erosion names this protection that living plants and their litter give the soil against wind and water. Plants make the soil more permeable to rain, which reduces runoff, and they shelter it from the wind. Their roots bind the soil and interweave into a solid mass that resists both water and wind erosion. Remove the vegetation and surface erosion speeds up. Increasing plant cover is the most effective known way to prevent both wind and water erosion.

soil-water-014.title: How farming speeds erosion beyond repair
soil-water-014.text: Over a third of the U.S. Corn Belt has lost its topsoil entirely. Unsustainable farming raises erosion one to two orders of magnitude above the natural rate, far beyond what soil formation can replace. Agriculture and soil erosion names this speeding up. The culprits are practices that loosen, bare or compact the soil. {{ref:soil-agri-095}}, which breaks soil into finer particles, is a primary cause. Mechanized deep plowing makes far more soil available for water to carry off. Growing one crop year after year, farming steep slopes, row crops and irrigation that runs water over the surface all add to the loss. So do pesticides and fertilizers that kill soil-binding organisms. Heavy grazing strips plant cover and severely compacts the soil. At farm sites in the Appalachian Mountains, intensive practices have driven erosion up to 100 times the natural regional rate. Potatoes carry a higher erosion risk than cereals or oilseed crops. Erosion is also selective by size: the finer eroded fraction loses more total phosphorus than the soil as a whole. Switching U.S. fields to {{ref:soil-agri-117}} would cut their erosion by more than 70 percent.

soil-water-035.title: Dust, the soil that travels on the wind
soil-water-035.text: Each year about 132 million tons of Saharan dust cross the Atlantic, reaching the Caribbean and the Amazon basin. Dust is fine particles of solid matter. On Earth it is mostly airborne particles from soil lifted by wind, from volcanic eruptions and from pollution. Dust that stays suspended in the atmosphere for a long time counts as an aerosol. Windborne dust comes mainly from grains bouncing along the ground in dry regions, as {{ref:soil-water-010}} describes. Strong winds there strip mostly silt-sized material up to 1/16 mm across. Grazing, plowing, vehicles and other human activity loosen these source areas further. Dust-producing surfaces cover about one-third of the global land area, roughly 13 billion hectares. The dust can affect temperatures and rainfall, and dust from erosion suppresses rain. Since the 1970s, dust events have been linked to declining coral reef health in the Caribbean and Florida. Soil dust is a major source of air pollution and often carries toxic chemicals such as pesticides or petroleum fuels. It poses a health risk to children, older people and people with respiratory diseases.

soil-water-045.title: Erodibility, or why some soils give way more easily
soil-water-045.text: Give two soils the same storm and one may lose far more than the other. Erodibility is the inherent lack of resistance of a soil or rock to erosion. A highly erodible material loses more for the same amount of work done by erosive processes. For soil, it is a lumped value for how a profile responds each year to detachment and transport by raindrops and surface flow. In the {{ref:soil-water-041}} it is the K factor, estimated from silt and very fine sand content, clay content, organic matter, structure and permeability. Clay-rich soils resist erosion better than sandy or silty ones because clay binds particles together. Organic matter helps by coagulating colloids into a stronger, more stable structure. Long cultivation depletes it and raises erodibility. Wet or compacted soils absorb less rain, so more water runs off and erodes. Stone cover protects against erosion, which matters greatly in Mediterranean countries. For channels and dams, erodibility can be measured with a {{ref:soil-water-094}} or a {{ref:soil-water-095}}.

soil-water-017.title: Warmer climate, heavier rain, faster soil loss
soil-water-017.text: Warmer temperatures are expected to intensify the water cycle, bringing more extreme rainfall and so more erosion unless measures are taken. Climate change and soil erosion names this expected rise. Studies by Pruski and Nearing suggest about a 1.7% change in soil erosion for each 1% change in total precipitation. Early 21st-century studies predicted rainfall erosivity rising by 17% in the United States, 18% in Europe and 30 to 66% globally. Other routes run through shifts in plant canopy and litter, loss of soil organic matter, winter snow turning to erosive rain, and thawing permafrost.

soil-water-015.title: What happens to forest soil when the trees go
soil-water-015.text: Deforestation and soil erosion names the rise in erosion that follows removal of forest cover and its protective floor. Clearing strips away litter and humus, removes the binding roots, and lets logging machinery compact the soil. After fire or logging, erosion stays low as long as the forest floor remains intact. Severe fires followed by heavy rain cause much more. Slash-and-burn clearing of tropical forest is one of the largest contributors to erosive soil loss worldwide. In Brazilian studies, runoff and soil loss fell to forest-like levels after 4 to 5 years of regrowth. Fifteen years of rest from farming restored the original soil. Researchers still debate which does more lasting harm to tropical soils: slash-and-burn with forest regrowth, or permanent pasture and cash crops after logging.

soil-water-013.title: Steeper and longer slopes, faster soil loss
soil-water-013.text: The shape of the land sets the speed of the water. Slope and erosion names the influence of a slope's steepness and length on how fast runoff flows and how much soil it erodes. That speed sets how erosive the runoff is. Longer, steeper slopes, especially poorly vegetated ones, erode much faster in heavy rain than short, gentle ones. Steep terrain is also more prone to mudslides and other gravity-driven erosion, including {{ref:soil-water-057}}. The {{ref:soil-water-041}} represents slope length and steepness with its L and S factors.

soil-water-004.title: Splash erosion, the first blow of the raindrop
soil-water-004.text: A single raindrop can fling soil particles up to 1.5 meters. Splash erosion is the erosion caused when falling raindrops strike bare soil and knock particles loose. Each drop makes a small crater and throws soil out of it. The loosened particles then move off with surface runoff. On level ground without wind, they can travel up to 0.6 meters vertically and 1.5 meters horizontally. Larger, faster drops carry more kinetic energy and throw particles further. Plant cover and crop leftovers soften the impact. Splash is usually seen as the first and least severe stage of water erosion, followed by {{ref:soil-water-005}}, {{ref:soil-water-025}} and {{ref:soil-water-027}}.

soil-water-016.title: Building cities, speeding erosion
soil-water-016.text: A construction site strips vegetation, alters the drainage and compacts the soil. Asphalt and concrete then increase both surface runoff and surface wind speeds. Urbanization and erosion names this increase in erosion and polluted runoff caused by construction, roads and paved urban land. Sediment in runoff from urban areas, especially roads, is often heavily contaminated with fuel, oil and other chemicals. The extra runoff changes how much water flows through nearby watersheds and how fast. It fills them with polluted sediment and greatly increases erosion of their banks.

soil-water-025.title: Rills, the first scratches of an erosion problem
soil-water-025.text: The first sign that a field is losing soil is often a set of tiny channels. Rills are shallow channels, no more than a few centimeters deep, cut into soil by flowing surface water, and rill erosion is the erosion that happens in them. Smaller incised channels are microrills. Larger ones are the subject of {{ref:soil-water-027}}. Hillslope runoff cuts rills into unprotected soil, as on farmland left bare, after deforestation or during construction. Rills are easy to see when first cut, so they often give the first warning of an erosion problem. Tractors help start them. They compact the soil so that water runs over it, and their wheel tracks channel the water into rills. Flow in a rill is typically a few centimeters deep or less, so its hydraulics differ greatly from flow in streams and rivers. It is still strong. Rill flow may carry nearly ten times as much as the interrill areas between rills. In moderate rain it can move rock fragments up to 9 cm across. Without conservation measures, rills can grow into those larger channels or, in semi-arid regions, into badlands. Under good management, contour tilling repairs them.

soil-water-027.title: Gullies, the scars a neglected rill can become
soil-water-027.text: On Madagascar's high central plateau, gully furrows commonly exceed 50 meters deep and 1 kilometer wide. Gully erosion cuts gullies: steep-sided channels formed in soil by running water, mass movement or both, usually on hillsides or on low ground that rivers flood. Most are meters to tens of meters deep and wide. Each has a distinct headscarp, the steep wall at its head, and lengthens by headward erosion at a knickpoint, a sudden step in its bed. Gullies carry water only intermittently, after intense or long rain or snowmelt. Many begin where a rill was neglected and kept growing. Hillslope cultivation, clearing, heavy grazing and tracks worn by livestock or vehicles start or speed up gullying. Inside a gully, flowing water cuts down and erodes the banks, walls collapse and groundwater seeps out. In dispersive soils, buried soil pipes collapse as well. Gullies cut farm productivity and supply sediment that chokes downstream waters. Losses are greatest in unstable, dispersive soils. They can supply 10 to 80% of total erosion on cultivated and grazed land, yet the {{ref:soil-water-041}} cannot simulate them.

soil-water-041.title: The Universal Soil Loss Equation, six factors multiplied
soil-water-041.text: Six factors, multiplied together, give a field's long-term soil loss. The Universal Soil Loss Equation, or USLE, is a widely used empirical model that estimates long-term average annual soil loss from water erosion. It multiplies rainfall erosivity (R), soil erodibility (K), slope length and steepness (L and S), cover and management (C) and support practices (P). It was built in the U.S. from erosion plot and {{ref:soil-water-256}} experiments, using data the USDA collected from the 1930s. Its standard unit plot has LS = 1, a 9% slope 22.1 m long, kept bare, tilled up and down the slope, with no conservation practice. K can be read from a nomograph using particle size, organic matter, structure and permeability, and LS from a slope chart. C and P must come from plot data. It is the most commonly used soil loss model and the main one used by U.S. agencies. It helped implement the multibillion-dollar U.S. conservation program. Though plot-based, it is often applied to watersheds, continents and the globe, and it cannot simulate gully erosion. Revised (RUSLE) and Modified (MUSLE) versions remain in use, and newer models such as G2 still build on it.

soil-water-043.title: Predicting erosion, and why the forecasts often miss
soil-water-043.text: Predicted and observed erosion rates often differ widely. Erosion prediction uses data and models to forecast where, and how fast, erosion may happen. There are dozens of models. Some treat long-term natural erosion as part of landscape evolution, while many quantify erosion sped up by people. Most predict average annual soil loss from a plot, field or catchment under different land management. Most consider only water erosion. Few predict wind erosion, and models of {{ref:soil-water-038}} or gully erosion are rare. Process-based models solve equations for detachment, transport and deposition. Empirical models relate soil loss statistically to environmental and management factors. No model is fully process-based yet. Research favors process-based models, but the empirical USLE remains the standard for conservation planning. Two widely used North American models are the Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation, RUSLE, and the Water Erosion Prediction Project model, {{ref:soil-water-111}}. Unless calibrated locally, models remain better research tools than regulatory instruments. They are also non-linear, which makes it hard or impossible to scale predictions from small plots up to large areas.

soil-water-254.title: Geotextiles, fabrics that hold the soil in place
soil-water-254.text: In the 1950s, R.J. Barrett laid fabric behind seawalls and under erosion control blocks and riprap. A geotextile is a permeable fabric laid with soil to separate, filter, reinforce, protect or drain it. Geotextiles were first meant to replace granular soil filters. Most are polypropylene or polyester, either woven or felt-like nonwoven, and they belong to the wider family of geosynthetics. They go into {{ref:soil-water-093}} and bank protection. As matting, they steady flow in channels and swales and let plants grow on steep slopes. Geotextiles of coconut fiber, {{ref:soil-agri-139}}, are popular for erosion control and for steadying slopes. They last about 3 to 5 years and then break down into humus.
